doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: The Abercrombie organ trio: risk-taking and bass responsibility
summary: They explain the trio's experimental approach, Wall's keyboard bass role, and how the music dictates what they play.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: When I listen to some of your recent recordings with this particular trio you’re working with with John, it really sounds like there’s a lot of experimenting going on almost at every moment. Is that just inherent in the music or do you guys feel like you’re really pushing the envelope of what an organ based trio can do?
I think that’s kind of what we tried to do from the beginning of this band really. That was the idea.

I think we all are very respectful of things that have gone on before and love that, and at the same time we all like to look. I think we all have some kind of vision and I think we all have very similar common denominators as far as our musical roots and understanding, and it’s like okay, we understand this and let’s see how we can try to test some new waters. I don’t think it was really a conscious effort, it was just kind of that we’re all of a similar mind I think. We all have that similar kind of attitude about okay, let’s reach. And that’s just I guess an unspoken thing that we like to do. We like to take chances, take risks. And because we’ve kind of developed a trust of one another within this situation, these potentials are there for things to happen. Sometimes they work out, sometimes they don’t, but that’s all part of the fun. Taking chances, I mean taking some risks. We don’t want to play it safe.
Right. And you’re like the bass player too.
He’s the every man. He takes care of everything.
I mean you have a — I can’t think of the word — but you can send the thing where it’s going to go.

He dictates a lot of what can happen. I think within the situation we all have a little more responsibility, which comes with the freedom, meaning more responsibility. I think very harmonically also. I’m understanding always what’s going on with the structures and how I can help to underline and give some kind of support to the harmonic structure of the compositions. You know not just with him but I’m helping to index those things, because there’s not necessarily a bass player and a separate piano player. And if I help to do that that helps to free him at times. And we all kind of like take turns extending into other zones.

Yeah it makes it, you know being the bass player, and I really feel this when I go back to the piano where I have a bass player, you know being the bass player really definitely creates more responsibility as Adam was saying, but actually I’ve learned to enjoy that responsibility because it gives me an ability to shape things for myself a certain way or to respond to something say Adam is doing so that it really takes a change of gears because basically you’re talking about the keyboard player and the bass player and one instantly going a certain direction. We’ve had a lot of fun with this over the years because we can just zoom. And it’s a good responsibility. And like Adam said, sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t. But when it works I think it’s an unusually good thing. And going back to when we put the band together we definitely didn’t sit down and have a meeting and say listen, let’s do something different than the traditional organ trio. I think that was just basically in the air when the three of us got together to play and especially started playing gigs, that was basically automatically there, that this is going to be, to play these

tunes, actually just even a great percentage of the material that we play if you played it as a traditional organ trio it wouldn’t quite work. It kind of dictates that, you know, here’s a piece of music—
The music tells you what to do.
The music really tells you what to do and then you have to figure out how to take care of it you know, just support what it tells you to do.
